Moral norm is positively associated with perceived non-economic benefits but not with perceived economic benefits, indicating a distinction between the two dimensions of perceived benefits. In addition, the interaction between subjective norm and moral norm is positive and statistically significant, indicating that the positive relationship between moral norm and transition intention becomes stronger as subjective norm increases. Research limitations/implications This study is limited by its cross-sectional design and its focus on transition intention rather than actual behavior. The model also does not fully account for socio-demographic, structural and institutional factors that may affect the intention-behavior gap. Future research should use longitudinal data, incorporate these external constraints, examine mechanisms that may bridge the intention-behavior gap and test the model across different geographical contexts. Originality/value This study extends behavioral research on organic aquaculture in three respects. First, it distinguishes perceived economic and non-economic benefits to provide a more differentiated understanding of benefit-related considerations associated with transition intention. Second, building on TPB and NAM, it examines subjective norm not only as a direct predictor of intention but also as a moderator of the relationship between moral norm and transition intention. Third, by applying this framework to aquaculture households in Thanh Hoa, Vietnam, the study provides context-specific insights for policymakers, extension agencies and other stakeholders in designing policies and support programs for organic aquaculture transition.
10.1073/pnas.2600502123: In a thermally stratified lake, freshwater fish select habitats that align with their thermal preferences. While most studies of dimictic lakes have focused on habitat selection during summer stratification, less attention has been given to winter when inverse thermal stratification occurs with water temperatures between 0 to 4 °C. Our results show that winter thermal stratifications vary considerably among lakes. Much of the variation in winter depth use by the cold-water predator, Lake Trout ( Salvelinus namaycush ), can be explained by the depth of the 2 °C isotherm. Selection ratios further support preferential use of this thermal boundary after accounting for habitat availability. Larger, shallower, and windier lakes tend to exhibit colder mean temperatures near 0 °C and deeper isotherms, typically within the 1 to 2 °C range. In contrast, deeper or more sheltered lakes maintained warmer temperatures close to 4 °C and a shallower 2 °C isotherm. Using multiyear acoustic telemetry of Lake Trout from 11 different lakes, we found that in warmer lakes with depth-averaged temperatures above 2 °C, Lake Trout used thermal habitat averaging 2.6 ± 0.6 °C, which occurred in relatively shallow depths (0.1 to 11.3 m). In contrast, in the one large, shallow lake studied, where maximum water temperatures were below 2 °C, Lake Trout occupied the deepest waters during winter (16.8 to 26.4 m) and experienced average temperatures of 1.5 ± 0.4 °C. Applying our model to 877,927 Canadian and Alaskan lakes predicted a roughly even split between warm and cold winter conditions; however, 73% of the 66,500 known Lake Trout lakes exhibited warmer winter conditions, where Lake Trout would occupy the upper water column during winter.
10.3897/neotropical.21.e212775: Tropical freshwater fisheries support both biodiversity and human livelihoods, yet long-term fishery characteristics data remain scarce across much of the Amazon Basin. Fish markets offer an opportunity to assess patterns in fish diversity and body sizes from exploited aquatic communities. Fish diversity and body sizes (standard length; SL) of common, locally harvested fish sold in Mercado Belén, Iquitos (Peruvian Amazon), were measured using photographic surveys conducted 11 years apart, in 2008 and 2019. Mean SL of the 10 most abundant species or genera differed significantly between these two years for seven taxa, increasing in five taxa (including Prochilodus nigricans and Plagioscion squamosissimus ) and decreasing in two, notably in a large, predatory Cichla sp. Taxonomic richness and diversity showed small declines between these two years. Minor differences in community composition were observed between years, but the dominant taxa were similar. These two time points serve as a baseline for future comparisons and by themselves do not demonstrate temporal or regional trends. Market surveys provide a useful, low-cost complement to field-based ecological studies in tropical freshwater ecosystems.
10.1139/cjz-2026-0108: Intestinal disaccharidases are key determinants of carbohydrate assimilation in fish. Here, we characterized maltase and sucrase activity in juveniles of Oligosarcus jenynsii (Günther, 1864) and evaluated the modulation of maltase activity by dopamine. Maltase activity was detected across a broad pH (6.0-8.0) and temperature (4-45 °C) range and followed Michaelis-Menten kinetics (Km :1.22 mM), whereas sucrase activity was not detected. In vitro assays showed that dopamine significantly stimulated maltase activity in a concentration-dependent manner, with increases at 10-4 and 10-3 M. This stimulatory effect was not observed in the presence of the D1 receptor antagonist SCH-23390 or the D2 receptor antagonist chlorpromazine. These results demonstrate that intestinal maltase activity is responsive to dopaminergic stimulation under in vitro conditions and suggest the participation of dopaminergic pathways in this response. The physiological significance of this modulation in vivo remains to be established. These findings contribute to the understanding of the biochemical regulation of intestinal disaccharidases in a freshwater fish species.
10.55885/jucep.v6i2.1231: The Consumer Cooperative Usaha Mandiri in Tanjung Binga Village, Belitung Regency, encounters challenges in valorizing underutilized grade C fish catches, while local livestock farmers remain reliant on relatively expensive commercial feed sourced externally. This community engagement initiative sought to enhance cooperative capacity by converting low-value fish resources into fermented feed ingredients within a circular economy framework. Conducted over eight months, the program utilized a participatory approach that included needs assessment, community engagement, technical training, technology transfer, production trials, and ongoing institutional mentoring. The initiative's unique contribution is the integration of fish boiling, rice bran addition, brown sugar and EM4 supplementation, anaerobic fermentation, and product development into a cooperative-based fish valorization model. The intervention enabled the transformation of underutilized fish resources into value-added feed products and strengthened members' technical skills and business management practices, particularly in financial record-keeping, production planning, and market development. Laboratory analysis indicated an energy content of 392 kcal, protein content of 73.97 g, fat content of 8.97 g, and carbohydrate content of 3.93 g per 100 g. This initiative provides a foundation for reinforcing local value chains that connect fisheries, cooperatives, and livestock production. Future initiatives should focus on formulation standardization, nutritional validation, feed safety assessment, economic feasibility, and regulatory compliance to ensure product quality and long-term business sustainability.
10.46989/001c.173408: Mandarin fish ( Siniperca chuatsi ) is an economically important freshwater aquaculture species in China, yet the maternal genetic composition of cultured stocks from different regions remains insufficiently characterized. To assess maternal genetic diversity and population structure, 120 individuals were sampled from one wild-origin population from Huzhou, Zhejiang Province (ZJHZ), and three cultured populations from Chizhou, Anhui Province (AHCZ), Wuhan, Hubei Province (HBWH), and Jiangmen, Guangdong Province (GDJM). Mitochondrial D-loop sequencing generated 118 high-quality sequences and identified 22 haplotypes. Haplotype diversity ranged from 0.543 to 0.805, and nucleotide diversity from 0.00604 to 0.01095. Three common haplotypes were shared by all four populations and represented 94 of the 118 individuals, whereas most remaining haplotypes were population-specific and occurred at low frequencies. AMOVA attributed 94.17% of the mitochondrial variation to within-population differences and 5.83% to among-population differences, with the among-population component being statistically significant (FST = 0.05831, P = 0.00196). Pairwise FST tests detected significant maternal differentiation between GDJM and each of the other three populations, whereas differentiation among AHCZ, ZJHZ, and HBWH was generally low. Overall, the four populations shared a broad maternal genetic background while retaining low-frequency variation within individual stocks. These findings provide population-specific baseline information for maternal-lineage identification and female broodstock management in S. chuatsi . However, mitochondrial D-loop data do not capture paternal contributions or genome-wide diversity. Broader geographic sampling combined with genome-wide nuclear markers and pedigree information will therefore be required for a comprehensive assessment of broodstock genetic structure.
10.1007/s00784-026-07252-5: To evaluate the effects of fish-scale-derived nano-hydroxyapatite (nHA) incorporation on the mechanical properties, surface characteristics, hydrolytic behavior, and color stability of conventional glass ionomer cements (GICs). Nano-hydroxyapatite synthesized from black tilapia (Oreochromis niloticus) fish scales was incorporated into Fuji IX GP and Riva Self Cure conventional GICs at 5 wt% and 10 wt%. Unmodified materials served as controls (n = 10/group). Flexural strength, flexural modulus, surface roughness, and color stability were evaluated before and after thermocycling. Water sorption and solubility were evaluated once, without thermocycling. Data were analyzed using ANOVA, Mann-Whitney U, and Kruskal-Wallis tests (α = 0.05). nHA significantly affected the mechanical and physicochemical properties of both GICs. The 10 wt% nHA-Riva group exhibited the highest flexural strength before (40.34 ± 6.84 MPa) and after thermocycling (38.32 ± 2.93 MPa), with the smallest median percentage change following aging (- 4.75%). In contrast, the 10 wt% nHA-Fuji group demonstrated a median percentage change of - 56.90% after thermocycling. Water sorption was reduced in the modified Fuji groups, with the lowest value observed in the 10 wt% nHA-Fuji group (2.05 ± 0.13%). Surface roughness increased with increasing nHA concentration and after thermocycling. Most modified groups exhibited color changes exceeding clinically acceptable CIEDE2000 thresholds. Fish-scale-derived nHA affected the measured properties of conventional GICs in a material- and concentration-dependent manner. Reinforcing effects were most evident in Riva Self Cure, whereas 10 wt% nHA was associated with a pronounced loss of flexural strength in Fuji IX GP after thermocycling. Although nHA reduced water sorption in selected formulations, increased surface roughness and compromised color stability may limit clinical applicability. As remineralization and ion-release behavior were not assessed, these findings should be interpreted as material-performance data rather than evidence of clinical bioactivity. Conventional glass ionomer cements are widely used because of their fluoride release and chemical adhesion but remain limited by insufficient mechanical durability. Bio-derived nano-hydroxyapatite has emerged as a promising reinforcing additive; however, evidence regarding fish-scale-derived hydroxyapatite in different commercial glass ionomer formulations is limited. This study demonstrates that reinforcement is highly material- and concentration-dependent, with improvements in mechanical performance observed primarily in Riva Self Cure, while increased surface roughness and color instability may restrict esthetic applications. Clinicians should recognize that nanoparticle modification requires formulation-specific optimization, and that remineralizing potential was not evaluated in this study, before routine clinical use.
10.56201/ijaes.v10.no10.2024.pg162.176: This study assessed the socioeconomic characteristics and constraints confronting fish farmers in three agricultural zones (Owerri, Orlu and Okigwe), of Imo State, Nigeria. Targeted population were fish farmers whose sources of livelihood were from fish farming using earthen and concrete ponds fish culture system. A structured close-ended questionnaires were administered, in a random sampling procedure to a total of one hundred and twenty (120) fish farmers who were selected for the study, with forty (40) each from the three agricultural zones in Imo State. Items on the questionnaires were organized, categorized and coded correctly. Data were analyzed using Statistical Package for Social Sciences (IBM/SPSS) software version 22.0. The results obtained indicated that majority of the fish farmers were male (75%) across the three zones indicating gender disparities which may be due to land tenure system. The active workforce is within the age bracket of 40-49 years (35%). Majority of the farmers are married and has large family size. In terms of tenancy, it was observed that most of the farmers are tenants in Owerri unlike the other zones. It was also observed that (38%) of the fish farmers possess tertiary education certificate. In the study area, 13% of the respondents identified lack of storage facilities for fish products as a constraint, In addition, 73% of the respondents attributed poor power supply as a challenge confronting them in the aquaculture operations in the study area. Similarly, 67%) of the respondents ascribed inability to access loans or credit facilities as one of the challenges facing aquaculture. Besides, 83% and 92% of the respondents ascribed high cost of feed and inadequate capital respectively as major challenges confronting aquaculture activities in these area. While 13%, 20% and 23% of the respondents believed that poaching, high cost of land and high cost of fingerlings respectively were the challenges confronting them in fish farming. Moreover, poor pricing of harvested fish (30%), poor water supply (13%) and lack of technical skills (87%) were some of other significant (p < 0.05) constraints faced by fish farmers in the studied areas in Imo State. Therefore to enhance the development of aquaculture in the state, measures should be taken to reduce the cost of fish production through subsidizing cost of inputs, giving grants, organizing workshops, trainings, seminars, field days, radio programs and the use of Extension Agents (EAs). The state government through the Imo State Ministry of Agriculture can establish Fish Demonstration Farms in the three agricultural zones to serve as fish skill acquisition farms, for regular training of fish farmers in the state. All these will definitely assist in the development of aquaculture in Imo State
10.3390/sci8110361: Background: The Arieș River basin in Romania is historically mining-impacted, and data on metal accumulation in its fish and the associated risk to consumers are scarce. Aims: This study investigated elemental accumulation in fish from the Arieș River and evaluated the potential health risks associated with fish consumption. Methods: A total of 40 fish representing five species were collected by angling between June and September 2025, after the legal fishing prohibition period. Eight tissues per fish (muscle, gills, liver, skin, bones, scales, eyes, and caudal fin) were analyzed by inductively coupled plasma-mass spectrometry (ICP-MS). Contamination and exposure were evaluated using the pollution index (PI), metal contamination index (MCI), estimated daily intake (EDI), target hazard quotient (THQ), and hazard index (HI) for non-carcinogenic risk, and carcinogenic risk and total carcinogenic risk (TCR) for carcinogenic risk. Species and tissue patterns were examined by multivariate analysis, including linear discriminant analysis (LDA). Results: Multivariate statistical analysis revealed distinct species- and tissue-related patterns in elemental composition. LDA differentiated species with an initial classification accuracy of 82.5% and a leave-one-out cross-validated accuracy of 72.5%, with Cr, Mn, Pb, Sr, and Ni having the highest contribution. Tissue discrimination was lower (approximately 60%), with Sr, Zn, and Cu as main discrimination variable. THQ values for individual elements and HI were below 1, indicating no appreciable non-carcinogenic risk under the assumed exposure conditions. The highest CR values were associated with Ni (nase muscle, 2.26 × 10-6) and As (nase skin, 6.28 × 10-7). TCR ranged from 3.16 × 10-7 to 3.37 × 10-6 and remained below 1 × 10-4, within the acceptable range. Conclusions: Elemental contamination in fish from the Arieș River was generally low, and species and tissue type influenced elemental composition and dietary relevance. Continued monitoring is advised, with seasonal sampling, inorganic arsenic speciation, and attention to species such as nase when assessing consumption risk.
10.3390/fishes11110654: South Korea’s olive flounder aquaculture industry predominantly relies on raw fish-based moist pellets (MP), raising concerns regarding marine resource use and environmental sustainability. This study compared the growth performance and economic feasibility of extruded pellets (EP) and MP through a 12-month feeding trial conducted at two commercial olive flounder farms in Wando, South Korea. At each farm, three replicate tanks were assigned to each dietary treatment. Economic feasibility was assessed using net present value (NPV), internal rate of return (IRR), and sensitivity analyses of key production and cost variables. Final body weight and survival rate were significantly higher in the MP groups than in the EP groups at both farms. In the baseline analysis without government subsidies, Farm A recorded an NPV of USD 793,446 and an IRR of 14.1% for EP, compared with USD 2,244,588 and 28.8% for MP. At Farm B, the corresponding values were USD 705,580 and 13.1% for EP, compared with USD 2,836,482 and 34.3% for MP. Although both feeding systems were economically feasible, MP demonstrated greater economic returns, primarily due to higher growth performance and lower feed costs. These findings highlight the need to improve EP performance and cost-effectiveness while considering the long-term sustainability of aquaculture feeding strategies.
10.3390/pathogens15111176: Viral nervous necrosis (VNN), caused by nervous necrosis virus (NNV), is a devastating viral disease affecting marine fish aquaculture worldwide, particularly during larval and juvenile stages. Although NNV has a broad and expanding host range, the susceptibility of greenfin horse-faced filefish (Thamnaconus septentrionalis) has not been established. To determine whether T. septentrionalis is susceptible to NNV, we investigated an outbreak of abnormal mortality in juveniles from a marine aquaculture farm in Rizhao, Shandong Province, China. A comprehensive etiological investigation combined bacterial isolation and identification, real-time quantitative RT-PCR (RT-qPCR), tissue-distribution analysis, histopathology, transmission electron microscopy (TEM), and RNA2-based phylogenetic analysis. Diseased fish exhibited characteristic VNN-like neurological signs, including spiral swimming, loss of equilibrium, anorexia, and body darkening. Several bacterial taxa, including Vibrio- and Tenacibaculum-related isolates, were recovered from diseased fish, indicating the possibility of bacterial involvement. However, the concurrent detection of abundant NNV RNA in neural tissues, together with characteristic neurological signs, compatible histopathological lesions, and NNV-like particles, provided convergent evidence supporting natural NNV infection. NNV RNA was detected in all ten diseased fish, whereas the other screened viral pathogens were not detected. Pooled brain-eye samples contained 4.62 × 108 to 1.33 × 109 NNV RNA copies/μg total RNA, and abundant NNV RNA was also detected in brain, spleen, kidney, and trunk tissues. Histological examination showed vacuolar and degenerative lesions in the brain and retina, and TEM revealed numerous non-enveloped, spherical virus-like particles approximately 25 nm in diameter in neural tissues, consistent with NNV morphology. Phylogenetic analysis of the RNA2 capsid protein gene placed the detected virus within the RGNNV RNA2 lineage. Together, the neurological signs, NNV RNA detection, compatible histopathological lesions, NNV-like particles in neural tissues, and RNA2 phylogenetic evidence provide evidence of natural NNV infection in T. septentrionalis. These findings document evidence of natural NNV infection in T. septentrionalis under aquaculture conditions, highlight the need for further investigations into pathogenicity and transmission, and provide a basis for VNN surveillance and biosecurity management in filefish aquaculture.
10.1007/s11259-026-11599-1: Global aquaculture is rapidly developing as a production system for aquatic animal-derived foods. Sustainable production in the marine industry is not only hindered by disease challenges but also limited by the use of synthetic drugs against these disease outbreaks because of their tissue accumulation, which leads to resistant pathogens. As an alternative, medicinal herbs are mentioned in aquaculture as eco-friendly and safe products for preventing pathogens, enhancing growth, and improving the immune system. Moreover, medicinal herbs protect aquatic animals from stressful stimuli, including overcrowding, high temperatures, and poor water quality. Given the increased need of the aquaculture industry for phytoconstituents and their potential sources, this review mainly focuses on providing information on the nutritional, biochemical, and physiological impacts and the action mechanisms of herbal medicines from the Lamiaceae, Fabaceae, and Asteraceae families on aquatic species. Recent studies indicate that nano-enabled delivery systems can substantially improve the performance of herbal compounds, and this review therefore highlights the growing potential of integrating nanotechnology with phytobiotics to enhance their stability, bioavailability, and functional outcomes in aquaculture. Emerging nanotechnological delivery systems, including encapsulation in polymeric nanoparticles, liposomes, and metal-based nanoparticles synthesized using plant extracts, offer significant advantages for improving the stability, bioavailability, and targeted delivery of phytobiotic compounds. Nanoencapsulation of essential oils and bioactive phytochemicals (e.g., thymol, curcumin, rosmarinic acid) has shown particular promise in enhancing their solubility, protecting them from degradation in the gastrointestinal tract, and enabling controlled release, thereby maximizing their immunostimulatory, antioxidant, and antimicrobial effects in aquatic species. Essential information is presented about phytobiotics from these plant families and their mode of action, mode of administration and dosage, and other vital issues for phytobiotic research in aquaculture. Importantly, the review suggests that the practical use of these green drugs requires further investigation to uncover the biological functions of active compounds responsible for growth, immune, and pathogen resistance across diverse species of aquatic animals. With analysing 162 peer-reviewed studies, this review provides, for the first time, a comprehensive comparative analysis of phytobiotics from the Lamiaceae, Fabaceae, and Asteraceae families, integrating their mechanisms of action, dose-dependent effects, nanotechnology-based delivery systems and emerging nanotechnological applications, while identifying critical research gaps and future directions for sustainable aquaculture. The knowledge derived from the current discussion provides an exciting opportunity for the practical use of natural drugs in aquaculture.
10.56557/upjoz/2026/v47i215945: Rainwater-harvesting ponds offer opportunities for freshwater aquaculture by enabling the additional productive use of existing water-storage structures. Nile tilapia (Oreochromis niloticus) is widely cultured because of its adaptability to different freshwater environments. However, evaluating its growth under site-specific pond conditions is essential for understanding its performance and the potential suitability of rainwater-harvesting ponds for fish culture. This study described the weekly growth of Nile tilapia (Oreochromis niloticus) cultured in a rainwater-harvesting aquaculture pond at H.H. The Rajah’s College, Pudukkottai, from September 2023 to February 2024. Fish received commercial feed daily, and average body weight and body length were recorded at weekly intervals over a 24-week culture period. The initial recorded mean weight and length in Week 1 were 3.0 g and 1.5 cm, respectively. By Week 12, mean weight had increased to 110.0 g and mean length to 16.9 cm. At Week 24, the corresponding values reached 550.0 g and 30.2 cm. Across the recorded observations, average body weight increased by 547.0 g and average body length by 28.7 cm. Both measurements increased in every successive weekly record. Weight gains were smaller during the initial weeks and larger in absolute terms during the later stages, whereas increases in length followed a steadier pattern. These results document a continuous rise in mean fish size during one culture cycle in the study pond. However, the absence of a comparison pond, water-quality measurements, fish counts, variability estimates and feed-utilisation data prevents attribution of the growth pattern to the rainwater-harvesting system or assessment of production efficiency. The observations indicate that this pond supported tilapia growth during the monitored period, while further measurements would be required to evaluate broader culture performance.
10.3897/bdj.14.e209360: Maërl beds, also known as rhodolith beds, are biogenic benthic habitats formed by unattached coralline algae and support diverse macrobenthic assemblages. In the Mediterranean, especially its eastern basin, information on their distribution, ecological condition and associated fauna remains limited. Maërl beds are sensitive to physical disturbance, sedimentation and organic enrichment, including pressures associated with aquaculture activities. This data paper describes the macrobenthic fauna associated with maërl beds located near and further from finfish farms in the Traxilos area of the north-eastern Corinthian Gulf, Greece. The dataset comprises eight sampling events and 328 abundance-based occurrence records representing 6,410 individuals. The paper also provides morphological notes on two polychaete taxa, Syllis nigricirris and the Neanthioides acuminata species complex, documenting variation in diagnostically relevant characters.
10.3390/aquacj6040056: Expanded polystyrene floats have been identified as a significant source of marine microplastic in oyster aquaculture, yet no certification criterion assesses the material that the certified alternatives shed. Gravimetric mass loss, normalised to a common exposed area of 7200 mm2, is reported under accredited accelerated weathering to KS F 2274 for eight float materials: expanded polystyrene at three densities, expanded polypropylene, three injection-moulded polymers, and a continuous-fibre basalt-reinforced thermoplastic composite. Specimens were dried to constant mass before weighing, so the quantity measured is a net change: an upper bound on particulate release, not a measure of it. Mass exceeded the initial value in all three stabilised expanded polypropylene specimens. At 3000 h the loss spanned a factor of 54, and every foamed material exceeded every non-foamed one, while tripling the density of expanded polystyrene reduced loss by only 25% (n = 3; p < 0.0001 across the foamed groups). For ten injection-moulded grades the accelerated ranking reproduced that of 2.5 years outdoors (Spearman ρ = 0.89), though the ratio varied from 0.4 to 6.3. A wear model indicates that the pure-polymer barrier providing water tightness contains 905-1180 g L-1 of polymer against 578 g L-1 for the laminate beneath, so the wearing layer, not the bulk material, may govern release in service.
10.9734/ajriz/2026/v9i4330: African catfish (Clarias gariepinus) is an economically important aquaculture species in Nigeria, and sustainable hatchery production depends partly on the availability of suitable male broodstock and good-quality semen. This study compared selected semen quality parameters of cultured and wild male C. gariepinus to assess differences associated with broodstock source. Six sexually mature males, comprising three (3) cultured and three (3) wild individuals, were examined. Semen was obtained through testicular extraction following dissection. The evaluated parameters included gonad weight, gonadosomatic index (GSI), milt volume, sperm motility, sperm concentration, sperm viability, sperm morphology, and semen pH. Descriptive comparisons indicated that wild broodstock had higher mean gonad weight (5.33 ± 1.20 g), milt volume (2.72 ± 0.10 mL), and sperm concentration (5.82 ± 0.23 × 10¹⁰ sperm cells mL⁻¹) than cultured broodstock, which recorded 3.50 ± 0.76 g, 2.58 ± 0.17 mL, and 5.56 ± 0.11 × 10¹⁰ sperm cells mL⁻¹, respectively. The percentage of active spermatozoa was also numerically higher in wild fish (69.17 ± 7.77%) than in cultured fish (63.33 ± 14.00%). Semen pH was 7.00 in both groups. Wild broodstock recorded a higher mean proportion of morphologically normal spermatozoa (88.00 ± 2.16%) than cultured broodstock (76.80 ± 12.95%). The reported statistical analysis, however, indicated no significant differences between the groups (P > 0.05). Qualitative characteristics, including semen colour, viscosity, and liquefaction time, varied between the two sources. These findings indicate that both cultured and wild broodstock produced measurable quantities of testicular semen with broadly comparable characteristics under the conditions investigated. Further studies involving larger numbers of broodstock and controlled fertilisation trials are necessary to determine whether the observed differences influence fertilisation success, hatchability, and larval performance. This study provides preliminary information that may contribute to broodstock evaluation and management in African catfish aquaculture.
10.29165/ajarcde.v11i1.1511: Water quality largely determines the success of Nile tilapia (Oreochromis niloticus) cultivation. This study assessed whether two campus ponds at Politeknik Negeri Sriwijaya Banyuasin, Indonesia, are suitable for tilapia culture, using physical and chemical water-quality parameters and a descriptive quantitative design. Water was sampled at three stations per pond (inlet, center, outlet) on two occasions, with duplicate measurements. We reported temperature, total dissolved solids (TDS), dissolved oxygen (DO), pH, ammonia, phosphate, biochemical oxygen demand (BOD), and chemical oxygen demand (COD). Mean temperature was 32.00 ± 0.43 °C in Pond 1 and 32.42 ± 0.51 °C in Pond 2, and DO was relatively high (6.53 ± 0.19 and 6.55 ± 0.20 mg/L). TDS was low (26.42 ± 2.07 and 30.50 ± 1.68 mg/L). Mean pH was slightly acidic (6.09 ± 0.14 and 6.15 ± 0.14): below the 6.5-8.5 range used for tilapia culture, but inside the 6-9 range of Class II in Government Regulation No. 22/2021. Ammonia (0.48 ± 0.06 and 0.41 ± 0.10 mg/L), phosphate (1.25 ± 0.08 and 1.36 ± 0.09 mg/L), BOD (8.84 ± 1.44 and 10.93 ± 2.79 mg/L), and COD (29.00 ± 6.64 and 35.67 ± 9.11 mg/L) exceeded the comparison values used. Both ponds therefore offer supportive oxygen conditions but are constrained by organic loading and nutrient enrichment. They should be regarded as usable only after water-quality management and confirmatory monitoring, including dawn-time DO, nitrite, alkalinity, and the analytical basis of ammonia and phosphate. Contribution to Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs):SDG 2 (Zero Hunger)SDG 4 (Quality Education)SDG 6 (Clean Water and Sanitation)SDG 12 (Responsible Consumption and Production)
10.3389/fmars.2026.1943975: Seafood constitutes a major pathway for the transfer of naturally occurring and anthropogenic radionuclides from marine ecosystems to humans. The Tamil Nadu coast, spanning the Bay of Bengal, Palk Bay, Gulf of Mannar and the Indian Ocean, supports intensive fisheries, aquaculture and seafood consumption while encompassing nuclear installations, mineral-rich coastal sediments, major ports, estuaries, industrial zones and riverine inputs that collectively influence marine radioactivity. This review critically synthesises current knowledge of radionuclides in marine fish, crustaceans, molluscs, seaweeds and other edible organisms along the Tamil Nadu coast, with emphasis on their sources, environmental behaviour, bioaccumulation, trophic transfer and implications for seafood safety. Naturally occurring and cosmogenic radionuclides (^210Po, ^210Pb, ^226Ra, ^228Ra, ^238U, ^232Th, ^40K and ^14C), together with surveillance-relevant anthropogenic radionuclides (^137Cs, ^134Cs, ^90Sr, ^3H, ^99Tc and plutonium isotopes), are evaluated with respect to environmental sources, sediment interactions, tissue-specific accumulation, spatial variability and radiological significance. Under normal/background conditions, across Tamil Nadu studies that quantified radionuclide ingestion dose, ^210Po ^210Po frequently represented the largest contributor among the radionuclides assessed, although the magnitude of exposure varied substantially with seafood group, tissue selection, processing state and consumption assumptions. Anthropogenic radionuclides were less extensively characterised and generally contributed smaller reported doses in the available surveillance studies; however, their relative radiological importance may increase substantially following accidental or off-normal releases. Comparability among studies remains constrained by differences in sampling design, target species, tissue selection, analytical methods, reporting basis, detection limits, seafood-consumption data and dose-assessment assumptions. This review therefore emphasises the need for harmonised, long-term radioecological monitoring integrating seawater, sediments, plankton, representative marine biota and commercially important seafood, together with robust QA/QC, whole organism ecological dose assessment and category-specific probabilistic dietary exposure modelling. Establishing spatially and temporally resolved baseline datasets will strengthen seafood-safety assessments, improve source attribution, support rapid evaluation of accidental releases and provide a more robust basis for environmental protection and coastal management along the Tamil Nadu coast.
10.3389/fevo.2026.1960019: Background Tropical coastal seascapes rely on ecological connectivity between mangrove, seagrass, and coral reef habitats to sustain fish biodiversity and fisheries productivity. However, identifying key fish species that facilitate cross-habitat energy flows remains challenging due to limitations of traditional survey methods in turbid, structurally complex environments. Methods We integrated environmental DNA (eDNA) metabarcoding with Random Forest (RF) machine learning to map fish assemblages across a mangrove-seagrass-coral reef continuum in Hainan Island, South China Sea. Results We detected 234 fish species across 78 families - a 4.03-fold increase over conventional gillnet surveys (58 species, paired t-test, t = 11.34, p < 0.001). Using RF classification, we identified 23 "connector species" with high cross-habitat fidelity, of which three super-connectors - Lutjanus russellii , Siganus fuscescens , and Gerres oyena - accounted for 47% of cross-habitat network flow. Simulated removal of these three species reduced overall network connectivity by 68%. The RF model achieved 90.7% accuracy (Kappa = 0.86) in predicting habitat occurrence from eDNA data. Variable importance analysis revealed a salinity threshold at 28 PSU and a distance-to-reef threshold at 2.5 km as primary drivers of community turnover. Our bipartite network analysis showed significant nestedness (NODF = 47.3, p < 0.001), indicating that generalist species disproportionately maintain seascape connectivity. Discussion These findings demonstrate that integrating eDNA with machine learning provides a scalable, high-resolution toolkit for defining functional connectivity and prioritizing species for ecosystem-based fisheries management in the Anthropocene.
10.1007/s12562-026-02042-0: Advances in captive breeding techniques are expected to increase the production of artificially reared glass eels of the Japanese eel Anguilla japonica and expand their distribution in the market. This development has raised concerns about the lack of clear distinction between hatchery-reared and wild individuals during the distribution process. We developed a practical method to distinguish between these groups using differences in external morphology and otolith chemical signatures that reflect rearing environments. Compared with wild individuals, hatchery-reared glass eels exhibited shorter body length, greater body depth, relatively longer lower jaws, and broader heads. Morphometric analysis based on landmark methods for head shape in dorsal view distinguished between the two groups with 98% accuracy. Analysis of otolith oxygen stable isotope ratios (δ18O) and Sr/Ca ratios revealed clear differences in environmental history. Notably, δ18O values were completely separated between wild and hatchery-reared individuals, achieving 100% identification accuracy. These findings demonstrate that a stepwise identification approach combining rapid, noninvasive morphological screening with high-precision otolith δ18O analysis supports the development of a field-applicable framework. This method is expected to contribute to traceability in Japanese eel aquaculture and to provide a fundamental basis for future monitoring and management measures.
10.3354/meps15367: Little is known about western Indian Ocean anguillid spawning areas. Marine migrations of 15 silver-phase tropical eels (1 Anguilla bicolor bicolor , 10 A. mossambica , 4 A. marmorata ) released off eastern Madagascar (2022-2025) were tracked using pop-up satellite archival transmitters. Tags remained attached from a few days up to 181 d. Two A. mossambica and two A. marmorata migrated for more than 100 d, travelling 660-960 km northeast into the South Equatorial Current (SEC) within a warm ~18-20°C band at ~14-20° S, confirming the inferred spawning region from larval drift backtrackings. A. marmorata reached furthest northeast into the Mascarene Basin. Two A. mossambica released at the same location near the SEC bifurcation migrated in opposite directions, one north and one south of Madagascar, suggesting that some individuals may occasionally be entrained in boundary currents that influence their offshore trajectories. All individuals performed pronounced diel vertical migrations, ascending ~200 m (15-20°C) at night and descending to ~900 m (5-7°C) during daytime. In the Indian Ocean, the deeper occurrence of cold isotherms could explain these greater depths compared with Pacific congeners, implying that temperature, rather than light, limits their deep daytime migration. Eels may descend into frigid 5-7°C depths beyond the thermal limits of most epipelagic predators. Full moonlight suppressed nighttime ascents by ~140 m, indicating that visual cues modulate swimming depths. Together, these results refine our understanding of tropical eel spawning migrations and their sensitivity to oceanographic conditions in the western Indian Ocean.
10.3354/meps15369: Groupers (Epinephelinae) are ecologically important reef predators and key targets of Indo-Pacific fisheries, yet quantitative data on juvenile recruitment across habitat types remain scarce. We surveyed juvenile grouper recruits (25-50 mm TL) across five benthic habitat types (branching/corymbose coral; coral crevice and ledge; dead coral with macroalgae; seagrass; coarse sand and rubble) at two reef systems in the Surigao Strait, northern Mindanao, Philippines, over six survey periods spanning the northeast (amihan) and southwest (habagat) monsoon seasons in 2016-2017. A total of 344 recruits representing five species were recorded. Coarse sand and rubble was the dominant recruitment habitat, supporting over half of all recruits at densities more than eight-fold higher than any other habitat. Species composition was strongly habitat-dependent, with Epinephelus fasciatus and Plectropomus areolatus dominating in rubble, Cephalopholis spp. dominating dead coral with macroalgae and seagrass, and Epinephelus ongus predominating on branching coral. Overall recruit density was nearly three times higher during habagat than amihan, with the seasonal contrast most pronounced on sand/rubble. This seasonal increase was driven by the two rubble-associated species, whereas recruitment of the species associated with vegetated and structurally complex habitats showed little seasonal variation. These patterns are consistent with basin-scale larval supply as the primary driver of seasonal recruitment. Protecting rubble habitats from physical disturbance, including dredging, sedimentation from coastal development, wave-driven mobilisation, and restoration interventions that consolidate rubble beds to promote coral recovery, and incorporating physical environmental drivers into reef fisheries monitoring is recommended.
10.3354/meps15368: Understanding the environmental factors determining colony distribution is essential for interpreting the recovery and spatial dynamics of colonial marine predators. The South American sea lion Otaria flavescens has shown population recovery and recolonization along the Patagonian coast during recent decades, yet the habitat characteristics associated with colony establishment remain poorly understood. We analysed colony distribution along the Patagonian coast of Argentina using Ecological Niche Factor Analysis (ENFA), a presence-only habitat suitability approach. The coastline was subdivided into 230 coastal segments (~5 km), and 12 ecogeographical variables describing coastal geomorphology and nearby marine conditions were assigned using GIS analyses, nautical charts, satellite imagery, and field validation. ENFA models incorporating colony abundance were developed separately for colony types and age classes. All models showed good performance (cBI > 0.68). Colony occurrence was primarily associated with geomorphological variables, particularly beach slope, absence of cliffs, nearshore bathymetry, and beach width. Breeding colonies exhibited lower specialization than mixed and non-breeding groups, indicating occurrence across a broader range of environmental conditions. In contrast, non-breeding groups showed relatively high specialization, indicating association with a more restricted subset of available conditions, while sub-adult males showed high marginality in some models. Several currently unoccupied coastal sectors showed high relative habitat suitability, identifying areas with environmental conditions potentially suitable for colony use. These results highlight the combined role of coastal geomorphology and proximity to potentiallyproductive marine areas in structuring sea lion colony distribution and provide information relevant for conservation planning under increasing anthropogenic pressure and environmental change.
10.3354/meps15365: Several factors influence space use by animals, including consistent individual differences identified in numerous taxa. Individuals may benefit from returning to the same reliable foraging sites because this minimizes search effort or intra-specific competition. However, consistency in space use may put individuals at recurring risk from anthropogenic activities within their home range. Previous tracking of the small seabird, Leach’s storm-petrel Hydrobates leucorhous , in eastern Canada demonstrated their wide foraging range and overlap with offshore oil platforms. Here, we examined the intra- and inter-annual consistency of space use in the context of foraging trips (trip duration, total trip distance, maximum distance from the colony, time spent foraging, locations of home and foraging ranges) in Leach’s storm-petrels breeding at the large (ca. 2% of the global breeding population) colony of Gull Island, Witless Bay Ecological Reserve, Newfoundland and Labrador, Canada. Individuals exhibited highly repeatable foraging space use within and among years. Importantly, consistent individual differences in space use led to consistent differences in overlap with oil production platforms, and we estimated that nearly half of the Gull Island population consistently flew through light and oil pollution catch basins during the breeding season. Within catch basins, one tenth of all tracked birds interacted with the surface of the water (i.e., where theoretical oiling risk would be high) or flew past platforms at night (i.e., when light poses attraction risk). These results will be important for future conservation considerations, marine spatial planning, and environmental impact assessments of future offshore developments.
10.3354/meps15366: Tidepools in sandstone reefs are dynamic habitats where environmental conditions and resource availability are strongly modulated by substrate structure, influencing resident fish assemblages. We investigated the effects of habitat complexity on the composition, relative abundance, and trophic ecology of tidepool fishes in a sandstone reef at the mouth of a tropical estuary in northeastern Brazil. We hypothesized that pools with greater habitat complexity would support higher number of fish and richness, and consequently a more complex trophic structure. A total of 162 tidepools were sampled during 6 field campaigns in 2018. Pools were classified into 2 categories based on substrate cover: structured pools (SRT) covered by algae, and simple pools (SMP) lacking algal cover. We recorded 5609 individuals from 15 species, with Scartella cristata , Bathygobius geminatus , and Entomacrodus vomerinus accounting for 92.3% of individuals and 68.3% of total biomass. As predicted, relative abundance, biomass, and species richness were highest in SRT pools during the rainy season. However, habitat complexity not only enhanced these metrics but also altered trophic organization. In pools, fishes segregated into 2 trophic guilds: herbivores and omnivores. Diet analysis confirmed algae and microcrustaceans as primary food resources. Our findings demonstrate that habitat complexity, particularly algal cover and refuge availability, drives both assemblage structure and trophic function in tidepool fishes, highlighting the role of habitat heterogeneity in maintaining diversity in tropical sandstone reef ecosystems.
10.1073/pnas.2616760123: Mollusks are able to secrete and repair the most diverse and complex calcareous tissues in the animal kingdom, yet the detailed molecular mechanisms of these biomineralization processes, especially for the deep-sea calcifiers, remain to be elucidated. Here, using an in situ experiment, we report a repair mechanism for acid-induced shell damage via biologically mediated vaterite formation in the deep-sea cold-seep mussel Gigantidas haimaensis . Interestingly, the mussels secreted and recrystallized amorphous calcium carbonate into vaterite to seal the acid-induced dissolution porosities within 30 h. Calcium and nucleation substrates were potentially supplied by the mantle, including calcium-binding proteins and hydroxyapatite. Calcium then reacted with readily available carbonate in the extrapallial space, whose precipitation can be promoted by the nucleation substrates. This rapid repair mechanism is likely an advantage in the habitat of these mussels, which are characterized by pulsed acidification events from the seeping fluids. Furthermore, our finding expands our understanding of the diverse biomineralization mechanisms by which mollusks maintain their protective shells.
10.1242/jeb.252974: ABSTRACT Freshwater habitats display highly diverse flow regimes and oxygen tension (PO2) dynamics, driving lentic and lotic fish to evolve distinct physiological strategies for sustaining oxygen supply capacity (α) under hypoxic stress and high energy demand. We hypothesized associations of α with metabolic traits that differ between lentic and lotic species: lower PO2 thresholds for maximum metabolic rate (MMR) and other physiological functions in lentic fish, and higher MMR and metabolic rate (ṀO2) at given PO2 thresholds in lotic fish. We tested this by comparing MMR, hypoxia tolerance and hypoxic tissue metabolite responses in the lentic Pseudorasbora parva and lotic Acrossocheilus fasciatus. Pseudorasbora parva had superior hypoxia tolerance [lower critical PO2 at maximum and routine metabolic rate (Pcrit-MMR, Pcrit) and lower PO2 at loss of body equilibrium (PLOE)] via enhanced α, higher liver glycogen, and hypoxia-induced lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) upregulation, while A. fasciatus exhibited higher MMR, matching lotic aerobic demands. Within each species, elevated α correlated with lower Pcrit-MMR, Pcrit and PLOE. Unexpectedly, α was uncorrelated with MMR in both species. Biochemical analyses revealed brain LDH activity as a key determinant of hypoxia tolerance in P. parva, while interorgan transport inefficiency causing brain lactate accumulation and glucose depletion limited hypoxia tolerance in A. fasciatus. These findings demonstrate habitat-associated shifts in physiological and biochemical coping mechanisms, highlighting the complex environment-physiology adaptation interplay rather than categorical divergence.
10.25258/ijddt.16.82s.131: Marine teleosts precipitate carbonate minerals in their intestines and excrete them, and these precipitates contribute an estimated 3-15% of oceanic carbonate production. Whether elasmobranchs form comparable deposits is almost unknown. This study compared the morphology and elemental composition of solid material recovered from the intestinal fluid of a teleost, the Indian oil sardine (Sardinella longiceps), and an elasmobranch, the Bengal guitarfish (Rhinobatos annandalei). Intestinal fluid was filtered, and the retained material was oven-dried and analysed by scanning electron microscopy with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (SEM-EDX). Calcium was detected in both deposits. The ray-fish deposit contained 27.47 wt.% calcium (15.27 at.%), 2.32 times the 11.82 wt.% (6.22 at. %) of the sardine deposit; the difference of 15.65 ± 2.21 percentage points was about seven times the combined analytical uncertainty. The ray-fish deposit was also richer in phosphorus (14.62 vs. 6.83 wt.%), whereas the sardine deposit was dominated by silicon (21.65 vs. 3.52 wt.%) and contained aluminium (7.82 wt.%). SEM showed rosettes of spindle-shaped crystallites and ovoid granules in the ray-fish deposit, and diatom frustules in the sardine deposit. Ca/P atomic ratios (1.45 and 1.34) were consistent with calcium phosphate, while the ray-fish deposit alone held oxygen in excess of oxide stoichiometry (15.1 at.%), consistent with an additional carbonate or hydrated phase. These results provide a first elemental comparison of teleost and elasmobranch intestinal deposits and identify the mineral-phase and replicated analyses needed to assess the role of elasmobranchs in marine carbonate cycling.
10.3354/meps15323: Unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs, or drones) have been used as a valuable tool for monitoring intertidal habitats, offering a safe, efficient, and cost-effective alternative to traditional field surveys. We compared the percentage cover of the mussel Mytilus galloprovincialis obtained from drone imagery and traditional in situ quadrat sampling across 13 rocky shores along the Portuguese continental coast. Drone surveys were conducted at 2 flight altitudes (2 and 5 m) and across upper and lower mid-shore levels. Mussel cover obtained from drone imagery did not differ significantly between flight altitudes, between mid-shore levels, or from estimates obtained using in situ quadrats. A Bland-Altman analysis showed a low average bias (~2% higher estimates from drone imagery) and no evidence of proportional bias across the range of mussel cover values, although the limits of agreement suggest that moderate variability may occur at the scale of individual observations. These results demonstrate that drone imagery provides estimates of mussel cover in open rocky intertidal habitats comparable to traditional methods, supporting its use as a reliable alternative for monitoring purposes.
10.3354/meps15303: Foundation species support fauna through a diversity of pathways which simultaneously act to structure complex ecological communities. The co-occurrence of multiple foundation species can increase the number and diversity of these pathways, which can subsequently augment community complexity. Marine macrophyte beds provide a prime example of co-occurring foundation species. Indeed, co-occurring seagrasses and macroalgae support fauna through several trophic and non-trophic pathways, such as the provision of epiphytic food resources and complex physical habitat. However, many knowledge gaps remain about how seagrass and macroalgae can simultaneously and differentially influence ecologically important fauna species. We conducted field surveys, grazing assays, and predation trials to determine how the seagrass Thalassia testudinum and the macroalgae Caulerpa paspaloides and C. prolifera differentially influence ecologically important grazer populations. Grazer abundance was consistent across seagrass, C. paspaloides , and mixed habitats when epiphyte resources were highly and moderately available. However, grazer abundance was significantly higher in C. paspaloides habitats when epiphyte resources were in low abundance. Grazing assays showed that the presence of epiphytes and the decomposition state of macrophytes moderate grazer feeding preference, suggesting that grazers may use C. paspaloides habitats for alternative trophic resources when epiphyte resources become scarce. Furthermore, we found no evidence to suggest that predation potential differed among habitats. Our study identifies pathways through which seagrass and attached macroalgae can differentially support fauna, thereby augmenting the diversity of trophic and non-trophic support pathways through which co-occurring foundation species structure ecological communities.
10.3354/meps15305: Invasive macroalgae can profoundly alter coastal ecosystems, yet their interaction with habitat fragmentation remains poorly understood in marine systems. Using intertidal rockpools as natural mesocosms, we investigated how invasion by the non-native brown alga Rugulopteryx okamurae and experimental habitat fragmentation influence community structure, ecosystem functioning and biodiversity on temperate rocky shores of the Gulf of Cádiz. Rockpools along a gradient of invasion intensity were subjected to controlled fragmentation treatments by creating bare substrate patches of different sizes, generating varying edge effects to mimic different levels of habitat fragmentation. Short- and long-term responses of macroalgal cover, metabolic rates (net primary production and dark respiration), photochemical efficiency and associated macrofaunal assemblages were quantified. R. okamurae cover increased over time regardless of fragmentation, leading to homogenization of macroalgal assemblages and displacement of the native calcifying alga Corallina officinalis. Fragmentation had limited effects, influencing primary production and photochemical efficiency but failed to limit the spread of the invasive species. High invasion levels were associated with elevated respiration rates and reduced macrofaunal diversity, whereas native algae maintained high photochemical efficiency even under strong invasion pressure. Over time, macrofaunal communities became more homogeneous, with diversity remaining higher in less-invaded pools. These results demonstrate that biological invasion can override habitat fragmentation effects, acting as a powerful homogenizing force that reshapes intertidal communities and ecosystem functioning across temporal scales. Our findings highlight the importance of early management interventions to prevent long-term dominance by invasive macroalgae in intertidal systems.
10.3354/meps15308: Reproductive success is critical for population growth and persistence in mammals. In long-lived, capital breeding baleen whales, such as southern right whales (SRWs) Eubalaena australis , reproductive success is closely linked to foraging success. Under changing conditions in the Southern Ocean, changes in prey availability may compromise foraging success and subsequently maternal body condition, with implications for calf growth and survival. We used uncrewed aerial vehicle based photogrammetry to quantify intra-season morphometric changes in lactating females and their calves in the South African population of SRWs to provide a contemporary baseline for reproductive investment. On average, calves grew at a rate of 2.7 cm d -1 and gained 0.066 m 3 in body volume d -1 , while lactating females lost approximately 0.27 percentage points of body condition d -1 . While maternal body condition loss was comparable to estimates from other SRW populations, calf growth rates appeared slightly slower. In contrast to other baleen whales, changes in calf morphometric traits were minimally influenced by maternal factors relative to day of year, likely reflecting limited variation in size and body condition among sampled lactating females. These findings suggest that maternal investment during early lactation remains broadly consistent across populations, yet subtle differences in calf growth dynamics may indicate emerging energetic constraints or local adaptation. Continued long-term monitoring will be essential to detect potential shifts in reproductive success under a changing climate.
10.3354/meps15301: Compound-specific stable carbon and nitrogen isotope analysis of amino acids (CSIA-AA) may provide novel insight into diet and its link to persistent organic pollutant (POP) accumulation in long-lived apex marine consumers. We compared how successfully bulk and compound-specific amino acid (AA) δ 13 C and δ 15 N reflected trophic ecology and explained biomagnifying blubber polychlorinated biphenyl (PCB) concentrations in 2 groups of North Atlantic killer whales with previously characterised diets (i.e. direct observation, fatty acid analysis). As anticipated, bulk and CSIA-AA indicated distinct isotopic niches. Trophic position (TP) estimates using δ 15 N Thr-Phe and δ 15 N Pro-Phe were most similar to direct observations of diet. Most trophic-source AA pairs produced lower than expected TP estimates, likely due to 15 N-enrichment of source AAs in high trophic level marine predators. Although the correlation was moderate to weak, source-corrected TP did predict biomagnifying PCB concentrations, with δ 15 N Pro-Phe providing the best result. However, ‘traditional’ trophic-source pair δ 15 N Glx-Phe failed to accurately predict both TP and PCB concentrations in killer whales. CSIA-AA is a promising tool to track diet and POP biomagnification but requires a better understanding of trophic discrimination and source AA 15 N-enrichment in odontocete tissues.
10.3354/meps15299: Long-term changes in species distribution and abundance reflect the combined influence of environmental variability and barriers to connectivity. We re-surveyed distribution patterns of the mussel Mytilus galloprovincialis Lamarck, 1819 along the Portuguese mainland coast to compare coverage between 1997 and 2022. Potential biogeographical discontinuities in coverage associated with the Nazaré Canyon, Lisboa-Setúbal Canyon and a sandy beach were examined. Spatial analysis across 30 sites in 4 regions (North, Centre, Southwest, South) in 2022 revealed a clear north-south decline in mussel abundance, with the highest cover in the North (36.1%) and a marked decline south of the Nazaré Canyon. Compared to 1997, the North maintained high abundance, while the Centre and South showed significant declines, matching the Southwest region, which remained low. The North had significantly lower sea surface (SST) and air temperatures and higher significant wave height. No interannual variation trends (1992-2022) were detected for the mean and SD of most of the physical variables (SST, air temperature, significant wave height, atmospheric and marine heatwaves) except for the SD of SST in summer, which showed a positive trend over 30 yr in all regions and higher values in the South. This may suggest greater climatic variability, which could explain the observed sharp decline in mussel populations from 36.5 to 1.6% in the South region. North of the Nazaré Canyon, mussel populations appeared resilient over 25 yr. The vulnerability of southern populations suggests a concerning trend consistent with declines reported for mussels elsewhere in the world.
10.3354/meps15292: Early pelagic larval stages play a critical role in shaping recruitment variability of Dungeness crab Metacarcinus magister , yet zoeal distributions across the Northern California Current (NCC) remain poorly resolved at broad spatial and temporal scales. We used depth-discrete Multiple Opening/Closing Net and Environmental Sampling System (MOCNESS) sampling during 4 winter research cruises (2018, 2019, 2022, 2023) to characterize spatial, temporal, and ontogenetic patterns in Dungeness crab zoeae across the NCC. Zoeal abundances varied strongly among years, with winter 2023 exhibiting orders-of-magnitude higher concentrations. Across all years and regions, zoeae were most concentrated in the upper 50 m of the water column, with abundances declining with depth and no evidence of significant diel vertical migration. Clear ontogenetic structuring was evident across the shelf: early-stage zoeae were concentrated nearshore, mid-stage zoeae spanned the mid-shelf, and late-stage zoeae were predominantly offshore. Regional differences in abundance were present but modest relative to interannual variability, suggesting that year-specific oceanographic and biological processes exert stronger control than latitude alone. Together, these results demonstrate that Dungeness crab zoeae are neither temporally nor spatially uniform across the NCC and highlight the importance of incorporating early larval dynamics into a mechanistic understanding of recruitment variability and fishery forecasting.
10.3354/meps15294: Extreme cold events are becoming more frequent and more intense. Whether species persist or perish hinges on 2 factors: the shelter provided by benign microhabitats and the physiological resistance of the organisms. In the present study, we recorded the body temperature of intertidal mussels Mytilus galloprovincialis inhabiting different microhabitats, including tidal pools, exposed rocks, and shaded rocks, during a winter extreme cold event to characterize the distinct thermal regimes. We also determined the metabolomic responses of the mussels to the cold stress using high-throughput metabolomics. Our results indicated that mussels inhabiting tidal pools experienced less extreme, less fluctuating temperatures and suffered significantly lower mortality. Metabolomic responses of mussels living in the 3 microhabitats showed different patterns, suggesting metabolomic plasticity across varying microhabitats. Mantel correlation analysis revealed that temporal metabolomic responses of the mussels were significantly associated with environmental factors. These findings suggest that the refuge effect of benign microhabitats and microhabitat heterogeneity can influence metabolic plasticity, offering insights into assessing and predicting species’ vulnerability to climate change.
10.3354/meps15295: Nursery habitats for many commercially and recreationally important fish species remain poorly defined, even for heavily exploited or well-studied stocks. Coastal fishing using bottom-contact gear degrades benthic ecosystems, including potential nursery areas. Blue cod Parapercis colia s -a culturally and economically significant coastal reef fish in New Zealand-has been fished for over a century, with ongoing stock declines; yet juvenile habitat requirements remain poorly understood. A dual-gear survey across the Marlborough Sounds identified 4 key habitats supporting newly settled and juvenile blue cod: mixed-biogenic habitats, horse mussel Atrina zelandica beds, shell-debris mounds and cobble substrata. Ensemble boosted regression trees (BRTs) revealed strong predictive relationships with low-relief, high-rugosity habitats. These juvenile habitats were restricted to the mid to outer Sounds and offshore banks, with none in the inner Sounds despite available structure. Adult distributions mirrored these patterns, indicating coupling across life stages. Ontogenetic habitat shifts were evident: transitional-sized fish (20-30 cm) occupied intermediate habitats between juvenile and adult habitats, while large adults (>30 cm) were associated with rocky reefs. Highest settlement occurred in offshore biogenic habitats, rich in prey and largely devoid of cannibalistic adults. In the Marlborough Sounds, large-scale spatial distributions appear to be constrained by larval supply, while the availability and quality of juvenile habitats limit recruitment locally. Loss or degradation of these habitats (particularly offshore mixed-biogenic habitats) represents a critical recruitment bottleneck. Protecting and restoring key nursery habitats will be critical to rebuilding blue cod stocks and supporting the long-term sustainability of this iconic fishery.
10.3354/meps15297: Persistent warming over the past 3 decades in the epipelagic Gulf of California has been hypothesised to reduce zooplankton abundance and shift community composition. These changes in the food web are considered potential drivers of recent population declines in several megafauna species. We tested the hypothesis that zooplankton volume decreased between 1984-1988 and 1997-2019 and euphausiid abundance between 1978-1985 and 2005-2019. Diel variability and seasonal temperature variation (cold December-June vs. warm July-November seasons) were the main modes of variability influencing zooplankton volume and euphausiid abundance. Generalised additive models indicated that maxima occurred under neutral El Niño-Southern Oscillation conditions and at intermediate temperatures. Quantile regression and density distribution analyses provided no evidence of a long-term decrease in night-time zooplankton volume or euphausiid abundance between periods. A semi-quantitative comparison with 4 landmark California Cooperative Oceanic Fisheries Investigations cruises in 1957 similarly showed no detectable long-term decrease. Overall, these results suggest that zooplankton standing stock has remained broadly stable despite sustained sea-surface warming, or that any decreases were too small relative to the dominant diel, seasonal, and interannual variability to be detected across the available oceanographic cruises conducted in the Gulf of California.
10.3354/meps15283: Kelps are brown seaweeds and important habitat engineers of ecosystems found throughout temperate and polar coastlines, which have been declining because of multiple stressors. Recruitment is an important process which combines post-settlement survival and growth of the juvenile life-history stages to reproductive adults and can enhance resilience and promote persistence. We examined growth rate and survival of juveniles of the numerically dominant kelps Saccharina latissima and Laminaria digitata on the Atlantic coast of Nova Scotia, Canada, in the northwest Atlantic. We manually seeded spores on blocks made of Oceanite TM (a mineral matrix designed to promote settlement), which we transplanted after 7 mo (July 2022) into kelp populations at 3 locations that differed in temperature and wave exposure. We also deployed unseeded blocks made of Oceanite TM and concrete at 2 sites in November 2021, during the period of in situ spore release. We used generalized linear modelling to examine the relationships of growth and mortality of manually seeded kelp juveniles with temperature, wave exposure and spore origin, and the growth and change in density of naturally seeded kelp juveniles with temperature, wave exposure and substrate material. For both species, the most significant predictor of growth rate for manually seeded sporophytes over the first 5 mo of outplanting was temperature, with observed patterns following those expected based on limited known optimal thermal ranges (mainly for adults). The main predictor for survival was temperature for L. digitata and wave action for naturally seeded sporophytes. Juveniles from seeded blocks with spores of S. latissima collected from sites separated by ~100 km had similar growth rates, suggesting lack of genetic differentiation at these distances likely because of stepwise dispersal. Our study underscores the importance of understanding the role of environmental conditions in regulating kelp recruitment, and can help inform enhancement or restoration efforts.
10.3354/meps15280: Small yellow croaker Larimichthys polyactis , commercially important in Korea and China, is a demersal species found mainly in the shallow Yellow and East China Seas. Given its demersal nature and semi-enclosed habitat, the species is vulnerable to climate change due to limited access to climate refugia. However, most habitat studies have focused on Chinese waters or on specific seasons, with limited consideration of Korean waters and seasonal variability. Here, we projected seasonal habitat changes for the yellow croaker for the 2050s under SSP1-2.6 and SSP5-8.5 scenarios using 4 species distribution models driven by outputs from a regional ocean climate model and incorporating 3 environmental predictors: bottom temperature, salinity, and depth. Our results indicate that yellow croaker habitats are projected to contract year-round along the Korean coast in the Yellow and East China Seas, while expanding in the central Yellow Sea and across the East China Sea during summer and fall. These changes were associated with contrasting spatial effects of bottom temperature and salinity: projected increases in bottom temperature were associated with an increased presence probability in the Yellow Sea but a reduced probability in the East China Sea, whereas decreasing salinity showed an opposite spatial pattern. Our findings suggest that the future habitat of the yellow croaker may shift offshore, reducing its availability along the Korean coast. These spatial shifts may affect Korean yellow croaker fisheries by potentially increasing vessel travel distances and operational costs.
